points: Humans make mass movement more frequent and faster by removing the vegetation that binds soil and absorbs water, by adding water or weight to slopes, and by removing support at the base of slopes.
Managing slopes can reduce the risk.
Removing vegetation also exposes soil to rain splash, sheet wash, gullying and wind, which strip it away. Slopes then become prone to creep, slides and mudflows.
Answers may cover soil erosion as well as mass movement, provided the link to slopes and gravity is made.

notes.h: Overgrazing: how it happens and its effects
points: Too many animals for the land's carrying capacity eat the vegetation down to the roots and trample the ground.
Hooves compact the soil and break the surface of peat, leaving bare patches.
Without roots, soil and peat lose cohesion. Rain runs off the compacted surface or saturates the broken peat.
Sheet and gully erosion increase, soil creep speeds up (terracettes deepen), and peat slides occur.

From the 1980s, EU (CAP) headage payments paid farmers per animal. Sheep numbers rose sharply on hill commonage in western Ireland, including Connemara, Co. Galway, and the mountains of Co. Mayo, Co. Donegal and Co. Kerry.
Overgrazing stripped heather and grass, exposed and eroded blanket peat, and sent silt into rivers, harming salmon and trout spawning grounds.

Responses: payments were changed from per-head to per-area; Commonage Framework Plans, from the early 2000s, set lower stocking rates; REPS (the Rural Environment Protection Scheme, introduced in 1994) paid farmers to farm in environmentally friendly ways.
Destocking: reducing the number of animals to the land's carrying capacity.
Rotational grazing, moving animals between areas so that vegetation can recover.
Fencing off degraded ground to let vegetation recover.

notes.h: Overcropping: how it happens and its effects
points: The same land is cropped year after year without fallow periods or fertiliser. Soil nutrients and organic matter are used up, and soil structure breaks down.
Crops grow poorly, the ground is left bare between harvests, and marginal and sloping land is ploughed.
Loose, dry, structureless soil is washed downslope by rain or blown away by wind, forming rills and gullies.
On slopes, ploughing up and down the slope channels water and soil downhill.

notes.h: Overcropping case study: the Dust Bowl
points: On the Great Plains of the USA, including Oklahoma and Kansas, natural grassland was ploughed up for wheat in the 1930s.
Severe drought then left bare, dry soil, which wind erosion removed (see the notes on Erosion by wind).
Many farming families were forced to leave.
The US Soil Conservation Service was set up in 1935. Shelter belts of trees, contour ploughing and crop rotation were promoted.
The Sahel is the semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara.
Population growth led to more cattle, goats and sheep concentrated around wells and boreholes, shorter fallow periods, more cash crops and more fuelwood cutting.
With droughts, notably in the 1970s and 1980s, the bare soil was eroded by wind and by the heavy rain of the short wet season. This process is called desertification.
Crop rotation and fallow periods, so that soil nutrients recover.
Contour ploughing, ploughing along the slope rather than up and down it.
Strip cropping, terracing of steep slopes, and shelter belts against wind.
Mulching and cover crops keep the soil covered between harvests.
Rice terraces of Banaue, Luzon, Philippines: terracing of steep slopes, over 2,000 years old.

notes.h: Deforestation: how it happens and its effects
points: Trees are removed for farmland, timber, fuelwood, roads and building.
Tree roots bind soil and anchor it to bedrock. The canopy breaks the force of rain, and trees take up water (interception and transpiration).
Without trees, more rain reaches and saturates the soil. Roots rot and no longer hold the slope.
Landslides and mudflows become more frequent, especially in heavy tropical rain. More sediment and faster run-off reach rivers.

notes.h: Deforestation case studies: Haiti and Central America
points: Haiti has lost almost all its natural forest, mainly for farmland and charcoal. Neighbouring Dominican Republic has far more forest cover.
In September 2004 Tropical Storm Jeanne caused floods and mudslides off the bare hills around Gonaïves, killing about 3,000 people.
Hurricane Mitch, October 1998: torrential rain over Honduras and Nicaragua caused floods and landslides, made worse by deforested slopes. About 11,000 people were killed.
A mudflow from the Casita volcano, Nicaragua, buried villages during Hurricane Mitch.
Historic forest clearance left Ireland with very little woodland. About 1% of Ireland was forested around 1900.
Forest cover is now about 11%, mostly in conifer plantations.
Clear-felling of conifer plantations on upland peat, and building forestry and wind-farm roads, can destabilise peat slopes.
Afforestation and reforestation of steep slopes.
Buffer strips of trees beside rivers.
Selective felling instead of clear-felling, and restricting felling on steep or peaty slopes.

notes.h: Construction and drainage on peat and slopes
points: Wind farms and roads on upland blanket bog involve excavation, dumping of spoil on the bog surface and interference with drainage.

Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway, 16 October 2003: during construction of a wind farm on a forested blanket-bog hillside, a peat slide of about 450,000 cubic metres moved into the Owendalulleegh River, killing large numbers of fish.
In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland, a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day, because no proper environmental impact assessment had been carried out.

Meenbog wind farm, near Ballybofey, Co. Donegal, November 2020: a peat slide during construction flowed into the Mourne Beg River and crossed into Northern Ireland, polluting a river system important for salmon.
Road and rail cuttings steepen slopes or remove support at their base. Building weight on top of a slope adds to the downslope force.
Leaking pipes, drainage and irrigation saturate slopes. Reservoirs saturate valley sides (Vajont, see the notes on Mass movement (mass wasting) processes and the factors governing them).
Mining spoil heaps are unstable (Aberfan, see the notes on Human interaction with the rock cycle).
Slope engineering: retaining walls, gabions (wire cages of stones), rock bolts, wire netting and rock-catch fences on cliffs.
Regrading slopes to a gentler angle, and drainage pipes to lower the water content.
Planning: hazard mapping, avoiding building on unstable slopes, and environmental impact assessments before building on peat.
Monitoring and warning systems.

keyTerms.definition: The number of animals an area of land can support without its vegetation being damaged.
Grazing by too many animals, which eats vegetation down to the roots and compacts the soil.
Cropping the same land year after year without fallow periods or fertiliser, so the soil structure breaks down.
A period when land is left unplanted to let its nutrients and structure recover.
Ploughing along the slope rather than up and down it, to slow the flow of water and soil.
The degradation of semi-arid land into desert-like conditions through overuse, drought and erosion.
The removal of trees, which loses the roots that bind soil and the canopy that intercepts rain.
Cutting down all the trees in an area at once.
A wire cage filled with stones, used to retain a slope.
Waterlogged peat that covers upland slopes and can burst or slide when saturated.

questions.prompt: Examine how human activities can impact on mass movement processes, with reference to overgrazing, overcropping and deforestation.
questions.model: Overgrazing: too many animals strip vegetation and compact the soil, so roots no longer bind it and rain saturates or runs off it. Peat slides and faster creep follow. Example: sheep overgrazing on western Irish commonage after the headage payments of the 1980s. Management: destocking, rotational grazing and fencing. Overcropping: repeated cropping without fallow exhausts soil structure and leaves ground bare; rain and wind remove loose soil and rills and gullies form. Example: the Dust Bowl of the 1930s on the Great Plains of the USA. Management: crop rotation, fallow periods, contour ploughing and shelter belts. Deforestation: roots and canopy are removed, so more rain saturates the soil and roots rot. Landslides and mudflows become more frequent. Example: Hurricane Mitch, 1998, in Honduras and Nicaragua, or Haiti, 2004. Management: reforestation of steep slopes, buffer strips and selective felling.

questions.prompt: Examine how humans interact with mass movement processes, with reference to Irish examples.
questions.model: Overgrazing of western Irish commonage after the headage payments of the 1980s stripped vegetation, exposed blanket peat and increased peat slides; REPS and Commonage Framework Plans later reduced stocking. Derrybrien, Co. Galway, 2003: wind-farm construction on forested blanket bog caused a peat slide of about 450,000 cubic metres into the Owendalulleegh River and killed large numbers of fish; the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland in 2019 for lacking an environmental impact assessment. Meenbog, Co. Donegal, 2020: a construction-related peat slide polluted a river system important for salmon. Forestry on upland peat: clear-felling and forestry roads can destabilise peat slopes; about 11% of Ireland is now forested, mostly conifer plantations. Management: environmental impact assessments before building on peat, selective felling, and restricting felling on peaty slopes.

questions.prompt: Explain how deforestation can increase mass movement.
questions.model: Tree roots bind soil and anchor it to bedrock, so without them the soil loses cohesion. The canopy breaks the force of rain and trees take up water through interception and transpiration; without trees, more rain reaches and saturates the soil. Roots rot and no longer hold the slope. Landslides and mudflows become more frequent, especially in heavy tropical rain, and more sediment and run-off reach rivers. Example: Hurricane Mitch, October 1998, over Honduras and Nicaragua, where floods and landslides were made worse by deforested slopes, and a mudflow from the Casita volcano buried villages. Example: Haiti, where Tropical Storm Jeanne in September 2004 caused mudslides off bare hills around Gonaïves. Reforestation of steep slopes and buffer strips of trees beside rivers reduce the risk.
